screens.title: Building User Interfaces for dApp Interactions
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on the user interface layer that sits on top of your smart contracts. Good dApp UI design hides blockchain complexity and gives users familiar, predictable flows. You will learn how to design input forms that map directly to smart contract parameters, how to present the lifecycle of a transaction so users know what’s happening, and how to structure React components to keep this logic modular and testable. We will cover concrete patterns — for example, using a number input for a uint parameter, and validating addresses with checksum checks — and practical UX rules such as disabling forms while a transaction is pending. I’ll also show how to provide accessible, responsive UI so people on phones and assistive technologies get the same clarity as desktop users. By the end you will understand the common interaction patterns you should build into every dApp and how a small set of reusable components can make those patterns consistent across your app. Think of this chapter as the bridge from on-chain code to human-friendly interaction: reliable inputs, clear state feedback, and maintainable components.

keyIdea.title: Bridge complexity to clarity
keyIdea.text: A dApp's UI should make contract calls feel like ordinary web actions: clear inputs, immediate status, and consistent components.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Building User Interfaces for dApp Interactions
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Building User Interfaces for dApp Interactions

Make blockchain transactions feel predictable: map inputs to contract types, communicate transaction states clearly, and compose reusable React components for maintainability.

In this lesson
Why it matters

Users must trust and understand transactions. Clear UI avoids confusion, reduces failed transactions, and improves adoption.

Who benefits

End users, wallet integrators, maintainers, and auditors all gain from predictable UI patterns.

Explore Key Topics
Three focused topics we'll cover with examples and component code.
Concept Map
Input Forms
Transaction Feedback
Component Patterns
Connections imply data flow: inputs → contract → feedback → refresh UI.
Coming up
We will build a TransactionFeedback component, refactor App integration, and practice accessibility and responsiveness checks.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives translate the chapter's guidance into practical skills you can apply immediately. First, you'll design input forms that directly map to smart contract parameters: choose the correct H T M L input types, add clear labels and placeholders, and validate values like addresses and unsigned integers. Second, you'll implement clear visual feedback for transaction states, so users see pending, confirmed, and error states, with hashes or concise error messages to help troubleshooting. Third, you will apply basic React component patterns: create small, reusable components such as a wallet connect button, account info display, and a generic transaction feedback panel so UI logic is separated and testable. Finally, you will consider accessibility and responsiveness: semantic H T M L, keyboard navigation, color contrast, and layouts that adapt to mobile. Each skill reduces user errors and increases trust; these objectives guide you to create dApps that are both practical and approachable. During the lessons you'll see concrete examples, code patterns, and common misconceptions to avoid. By practicing these objectives you will make dApp flows predictable and easier to maintain.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Checkpoints
screens.narratorSegment: These applied checkpoints turn the earlier objectives into testable steps you can check in code reviews or QA tests. First, implement client-side validation: verify addresses look like Ethereum addresses and that numeric inputs are positive integers. Second, wire state transitions so that when a user confirms a wallet prompt the UI disables inputs and shows a pending message; when the transaction confirms update balances and lists automatically. Third, extract a TransactionFeedback component that accepts status, hash, and error props so all pages show consistent messages. Fourth, ensure accessibility: use semantic labels, aria attributes for status messages, and responsive layout so forms remain usable on smaller screens. Each checkpoint is small and measurable: you can run through them during manual testing. These skills help prevent common user mistakes like entering an address with a typo or resubmitting while a transaction is still pending. Treat these as lightweight acceptance criteria for dApp features.

screens.title: Designing Intuitive Input Forms
screens.narratorSegment: Designing input forms for smart contract functions is about translation. The UI must translate human intent into correctly typed values the contract expects. Start by identifying each parameter type and picking the clearest H T M L control. For a string use a text input and give a helpful placeholder; for a uint prefer a number input or a numeric text input with inputmode set to numeric to support mobile keyboards. For addresses use a text input but add client-side validation: check the 0x prefix and length, and where possible perform a checksum validation to catch common typos. Labels are critical: name fields like "Recipient address" or "Amount (ETH)" and include unit selectors for tokens. Provide inline hints for units or gas considerations. A common pitfall is allowing free text for amounts or addresses without blocking submission; that leads to failed transactions and frustrated users. Include required attributes and disable submission until validation passes. Example: a transfer function transfer(address recipient, uint amount) benefits from a two-field form where the amount field offers a unit selector (ETH vs token) and the address field validates checksum. Finally, show concise validation errors next to fields rather than modal alerts. This reduces friction and keeps the user in context. What concrete check will you add first to your forms?

keyIdea.title: Match types to controls
keyIdea.text: Choosing proper input types and early client-side validation prevents common blockchain mistakes and improves trust.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Designing Intuitive Input Forms
Definition

Map contract parameters to clear inputs

Selecting the right control and validating before submission reduces failed transactions and user frustration.

Rules of thumb
  • String → text input with placeholder.
  • uint → number input or numeric text input with inputmode.
  • address → text input + checksum validation.
  • Token amounts → unit selector (ETH / token).
Common mistake
Allowing free-form amounts or addresses without validation causes on-chain failures and lost gas cost for users.
Key Takeaway

Map types to controls and validate early. Clear labels and placeholders reduce mistakes.

Form Example
transfer(recipient, amount)
Recipient address (text, checksum validated)
Amount (number) + unit selector (ETH / token)
Example validation
// Validate an address: basic checks
function isLikelyAddress(input) {
  if (!input) return false;
  return input.startsWith('0x') && input.length === 42;
}

// For production use, perform checksum validation per EIP-55.
Try adding required attributes and disabling the submit control until validation passes. That single change avoids accidental on-chain failures.

screens.title: Transaction States and User Feedback
screens.narratorSegment: Blockchain transactions are asynchronous and can take time or fail. A reliable UI represents the transaction lifecycle in four clear states: initial, pending, success, and error. Initial state is when the user composes inputs and the main action button is enabled; labels should clearly describe the intent, such as "Mint NFT" or "Send Funds." When the wallet prompt appears and the user confirms, switch to pending: disable inputs and the action button, and display a persistent pending message with the transaction hash so users can track progress on a block explorer. On success, update relevant UI elements automatically — refresh balances, NFT lists, or counters — and show a green confirmation message. For errors — user rejection, revert, or out-of-gas — present a concise red error with any available reason to help troubleshooting. A helpful component will centralize these transitions and accept props such as transactionStatus, hash, and error. A common misconception is treating the wallet confirmation as final; always wait for an on-chain confirmation event before showing success. Also avoid overwhelming users with raw error traces; summarize the cause and provide a retry path. Which state transition will you wire first in your dApp?

keyIdea.title: Explicit state model
keyIdea.text: Represent every transaction phase clearly and update the UI only after reliable signals to avoid misleading users.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Transaction States and User Feedback
State Model
Initial
Inputs enabled, clear action label, ready to start.
Pending
Disable form, show "Transaction Pending..." and transaction hash for tracking.
Success
Confirm to user, refresh related data (balances, lists).
Error
Show concise error. Offer retry path and do not expose long raw traces.
Process Steps
1. Click action. Button labeled for intent.
2. Wallet prompt. Show 'Waiting for wallet'.
3. Pending. Disable inputs and show hash text for tracking.
4. Confirm / Error. Update UI and show short message.
Example message formats
Transaction Pending... Hash: 0x1234...abcd (copy visible as text)
Transaction Confirmed! Balance updated.
Transaction Failed: out of gas. Please retry with higher gas limit.

screens.title: Validating Addresses and Numeric Inputs
screens.narratorSegment: Address and numeric inputs require different validation strategies and different UX affordances. For numeric values like a uint256 you want to prevent decimals if the contract expects whole units, enforce positivity, and optionally cap values where reasonable to avoid accidental huge transfers. Use number inputs or numeric text inputs with inputmode to improve mobile entry. For addresses, visual validation focuses on format: check 0x prefix and length, and when possible perform EIP-55 checksum validation to catch typos. UX differences matter: numeric fields benefit from spinners, unit selectors, and immediate arithmetic hints, while address fields benefit from copy/paste helpers, checksum checks, and identity hints such as ENS resolution where available. A common misconception is trusting any value that looks like an address; checksum validation and clear confirmation reduce the risk of sending assets to mistyped addresses. Example: in a two-field transfer form, disable the submit button until both the numeric amount and the address validation pass. Showing the truncated address with an option to reveal full value helps users confirm without overwhelming the interface. Which validation will you wire first in your app?

keyIdea.title: Different inputs, different UX
keyIdea.text: Apply numeric guards for amounts and checksum/format checks for addresses; support copy/paste and unit hints.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Validating Addresses and Numeric Inputs
Address Input
Checks: 0x prefix, 42 characters, optional EIP-55 checksum to catch typos. UX: show truncated address for confirmation, provide paste helpers, and show validation inline.
Example rule
// Basic address check
const isLikelyAddress = (s) => s && s.startsWith('0x') && s.length === 42;
Mistake to avoid
Accepting any 42-char string without checksum or confirmation leads to irreversible asset loss.
Numeric Input
Checks: positive integer, no decimals if not permitted, reasonable upper bound. UX: unit selector, inline conversion hints, and blocking submission on invalid input.
Example rule
// Ensure whole number and positive
function isValidUint(value) {
  return /^\d+$/.test(String(value)) && BigInt(value) >= 0n;
}
Pro tip
Add a unit selector to clarify whether the amount is in ETH, Gwei, or a token's smallest unit.

screens.title: TransactionFeedback Component
screens.narratorSegment: A TransactionFeedback component centralizes how your app displays transaction states and reduces duplicated logic across pages. The component accepts a transactionStatus prop with values such as pending, success, error, and cancelled; a hash prop for the transaction id; and an error prop with a concise message. In practice, you return null when there is no status, and render a styled message area otherwise. Show the hash as plain text for copy or reference, not as an interactive external link, unless you explicitly build a safe link handler. Keep messages short and actionable: for pending, say "Transaction Pending..." and show the hash; for success, say "Transaction Confirmed!" and trigger any necessary UI refresh; for error, summarize the reason and offer retry guidance. In the code example on the screen you will see a clear mapping from status to presentation class names and a helper to truncate the hash for readability. Extract the styling to a small C S S module or Tailwind classes so the component remains framework-agnostic. One common mistake is exposing raw error stacks—avoid that and give users clear next steps instead.

keyIdea.text: Encapsulate status messaging in a component that receives status, hash, and error to present consistent messages.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › TransactionFeedback Component
Component Purpose
A single component that maps status to readable messages and small visual cues. It reduces duplication and ensures consistent UX across the dApp.
Code Example
// src/components/TransactionFeedback.jsx
const TransactionFeedback = ({ status, hash, error }) => {
  if (!status) return null;

  const getMessage = () => {
    switch (status) {
      case 'pending': return 'Transaction Pending...';
      case 'success': return 'Transaction Confirmed!';
      case 'error': return 'Transaction Failed!';
      case 'cancelled': return 'Transaction Cancelled!';
      default: return '';
    }
  };

  const truncate = (h) => h ? `${h.substring(0,6)}...${h.substring(h.length-4)}` : '';

  return (
    /* Render a non-interactive message block showing message, truncated hash, and short error */
    null
  );
};
UI guideline
Show the hash as visible text so users can copy it to a block explorer if they choose. Do not show long raw error traces; summarize the cause instead.
Visual Variants
Pending: amber band, message + hash
Success: green band, confirmation and refresh hint
Error: red band, short help text
Key Takeaway

Centralize transaction messaging so every page offers consistent, actionable feedback.

screens.title: Integrating TransactionFeedback into App.jsx
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating a TransactionFeedback component into your application involves two practical steps: wiring UI state to the component and disabling inputs while transactions are in-flight. In App. jsx you typically have state such as isSendingTransaction, transactionStatus, and transactionHash from a hook or context. When a user submits a form, call the function that sends the transaction and immediately set the pending state. Disable the form and submit button by binding their disabled attributes to isSendingTransaction. Pass transactionStatus, transactionHash, and any short error to TransactionFeedback so the same component presents the state to the user. The example from the chapter shows a simple flow: connect wallet, show account and balance, render a form that sets new data, and then render TransactionFeedback below the form. A useful pattern is to clear form inputs only after the transaction is sent, not before, to avoid losing the user's input if the send fails. Finally, treat a wallet rejection as a cancelled state and display a short message. This approach keeps users informed, reduces duplicate submissions, and creates a single place to update feedback styling or behavior.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Integrating TransactionFeedback into App.jsx
Integration pattern
Keep transaction state in a hook or context and feed it to UI components. Disable form controls while sending to prevent duplicates.
App.jsx snippet (illustrative)
// in App.jsx (pseudo-code representation)
const { currentAccount, isMetaMaskInstalled, ethBalance } = useWeb3();
const { isSendingTransaction, transactionStatus, transactionHash, sendTx } = useSimpleStorage();

// On submit:
// if (!currentAccount) alert('connect');
// await sendTx(data);

// Render form with disabled={isSendingTransaction}
// Render TransactionFeedback with status={transactionStatus} hash={transactionHash} error={error}
Practical tip
Do not clear inputs until after a transaction is successfully broadcast. That preserves data for retry if the send fails.
UX checklist
  • Disable form & button when isSendingTransaction is true.
  • Show a clear "Waiting for wallet" prompt before pending state.
  • Render transaction hash as text and show concise success or error messages.
  • Categorize wallet rejection as a cancellable state so users can retry.
Key Takeaway

Wire transaction state into form controls and feedback components for a coherent user experience.

screens.title: React Component Patterns for dApps
screens.narratorSegment: Using small, focused React components keeps your dApp maintainable and consistent. The chapter recommends a set of common components: WalletConnectButton encapsulates detection and connection logic; AccountInfo displays the connected address, balance, and network; TransactionFeedback presents status messages; ContractInteractionForm handles inputs and submission for a specific contract function. Each component has a single responsibility: WalletConnectButton should not render transaction state, and TransactionFeedback should not manage wallet connection. This separation of concerns makes testing and reuse straightforward. For example, reuse TransactionFeedback across pages that submit different transactions; it simply accepts status props. Another useful pattern is placing web3 hooks and context providers near the app root; components then consume the current account and network without duplicating logic. A common mistake is embedding web3 calls inside deeply nested UI components; keep business logic in hooks or the context so components remain declarative. By following these patterns you get code that is easier to audit, extend, and style consistently across the application. React Component Patterns for dApps means break dapp ui into focused components and move web3 logic into hooks or context for reuse and testability.. In practical terms, organize small, focused components for wallet, account, feedback, and contract forms. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › React Component Patterns for dApps
Component Catalog
WalletConnectButton
Detects wallet presence and initiates connection. Keeps logic isolated and retryable.
AccountInfo
Shows truncated address, balance, and network. Reads from context or hook.
ContractInteractionForm
Encapsulates inputs, validation, and submission for a single contract function.
Pattern advice
  • Keep UI components declarative; move side-effects into hooks.
  • Compose small components; reuse TransactionFeedback across flows.
  • Place web3 provider at app root so components remain simple.
Common pitfall
Mixing wallet connect logic with form rendering makes components hard to maintain and test.

screens.title: Accessibility and Responsiveness
screens.narratorSegment: Accessibility and responsiveness are non-negotiable for production dApps. Accessibility means using semantic H T M L, labeling inputs with clear elements, exposing status messages with aria-live regions, and ensuring keyboard navigability so users who cannot use a mouse can still perform transactions. Color contrast matters—use high-contrast text for status bands and avoid conveying meaning solely by color. Responsiveness ensures forms and feedback render and remain usable on phones and tablets: use fluid layouts, stack form fields vertically on narrow screens, and provide large tappable targets for key actions. The chapter encourages testing with keyboard-only navigation and a mobile viewport to catch layout collapses and truncated labels. A common misconception is that blockchain users are only developers; many end users will interact on phones or with assistive tech. Make the form fields correctly labeled, ensure the main action is reachable by the keyboard, and put critical status text inside an aria-live polite region so screen readers announce pending and success states without being disruptive. These practices increase adoption and reduce user errors. Accessibility and Responsiveness means use semantic html, aria attributes, and responsive layouts so all users can interact with your dapp reliably.. In practical terms, make dapps usable across devices and by assistive technologies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on the user interface layer that sits on top of your smart contracts. Good dApp UI design hides blockchain complexity and gives users familiar, predictable flows. You will learn how to design input forms that map directly to smart contract parameters, how to present the lifecycle of a transaction so users know what’s happening, and how to structure React components to keep this logic modular and testable. We will cover concrete patterns — for example, using a number input for a uint parameter, and validating addresses with checksum checks — and practical UX rules such as disabling forms while a transaction is pending. I’ll also show how to provide accessible, responsive UI so people on phones and assistive technologies get the same clarity as desktop users. By the end you will understand the common interaction patterns you should build into every dApp and how a small set of reusable components can make those patterns consistent across your app. Think of this chapter as the bridge from on-chain code to human-friendly interaction: reliable inputs, clear state feedback, and maintainable components.

These objectives translate the chapter's guidance into practical skills you can apply immediately. First, you'll design input forms that directly map to smart contract parameters: choose the correct H T M L input types, add clear labels and placeholders, and validate values like addresses and unsigned integers. Second, you'll implement clear visual feedback for transaction states, so users see pending, confirmed, and error states, with hashes or concise error messages to help troubleshooting. Third, you will apply basic React component patterns: create small, reusable components such as a wallet connect button, account info display, and a generic transaction feedback panel so UI logic is separated and testable. Finally, you will consider accessibility and responsiveness: semantic H T M L, keyboard navigation, color contrast, and layouts that adapt to mobile. Each skill reduces user errors and increases trust; these objectives guide you to create dApps that are both practical and approachable. During the lessons you'll see concrete examples, code patterns, and common misconceptions to avoid. By practicing these objectives you will make dApp flows predictable and easier to maintain.

These applied checkpoints turn the earlier objectives into testable steps you can check in code reviews or QA tests. First, implement client-side validation: verify addresses look like Ethereum addresses and that numeric inputs are positive integers. Second, wire state transitions so that when a user confirms a wallet prompt the UI disables inputs and shows a pending message; when the transaction confirms update balances and lists automatically. Third, extract a TransactionFeedback component that accepts status, hash, and error props so all pages show consistent messages. Fourth, ensure accessibility: use semantic labels, aria attributes for status messages, and responsive layout so forms remain usable on smaller screens. Each checkpoint is small and measurable: you can run through them during manual testing. These skills help prevent common user mistakes like entering an address with a typo or resubmitting while a transaction is still pending. Treat these as lightweight acceptance criteria for dApp features.

Designing input forms for smart contract functions is about translation. The UI must translate human intent into correctly typed values the contract expects. Start by identifying each parameter type and picking the clearest H T M L control. For a string use a text input and give a helpful placeholder; for a uint prefer a number input or a numeric text input with inputmode set to numeric to support mobile keyboards. For addresses use a text input but add client-side validation: check the 0x prefix and length, and where possible perform a checksum validation to catch common typos. Labels are critical: name fields like "Recipient address" or "Amount (ETH)" and include unit selectors for tokens. Provide inline hints for units or gas considerations. A common pitfall is allowing free text for amounts or addresses without blocking submission; that leads to failed transactions and frustrated users. Include required attributes and disable submission until validation passes. Example: a transfer function transfer(address recipient, uint amount) benefits from a two-field form where the amount field offers a unit selector (ETH vs token) and the address field validates checksum. Finally, show concise validation errors next to fields rather than modal alerts. This reduces friction and keeps the user in context. What concrete check will you add first to your forms?

Blockchain transactions are asynchronous and can take time or fail. A reliable UI represents the transaction lifecycle in four clear states: initial, pending, success, and error. Initial state is when the user composes inputs and the main action button is enabled; labels should clearly describe the intent, such as "Mint NFT" or "Send Funds." When the wallet prompt appears and the user confirms, switch to pending: disable inputs and the action button, and display a persistent pending message with the transaction hash so users can track progress on a block explorer. On success, update relevant UI elements automatically — refresh balances, NFT lists, or counters — and show a green confirmation message. For errors — user rejection, revert, or out-of-gas — present a concise red error with any available reason to help troubleshooting. A helpful component will centralize these transitions and accept props such as transactionStatus, hash, and error. A common misconception is treating the wallet confirmation as final; always wait for an on-chain confirmation event before showing success. Also avoid overwhelming users with raw error traces; summarize the cause and provide a retry path. Which state transition will you wire first in your dApp?

Address and numeric inputs require different validation strategies and different UX affordances. For numeric values like a uint256 you want to prevent decimals if the contract expects whole units, enforce positivity, and optionally cap values where reasonable to avoid accidental huge transfers. Use number inputs or numeric text inputs with inputmode to improve mobile entry. For addresses, visual validation focuses on format: check 0x prefix and length, and when possible perform EIP-55 checksum validation to catch typos. UX differences matter: numeric fields benefit from spinners, unit selectors, and immediate arithmetic hints, while address fields benefit from copy/paste helpers, checksum checks, and identity hints such as ENS resolution where available. A common misconception is trusting any value that looks like an address; checksum validation and clear confirmation reduce the risk of sending assets to mistyped addresses. Example: in a two-field transfer form, disable the submit button until both the numeric amount and the address validation pass. Showing the truncated address with an option to reveal full value helps users confirm without overwhelming the interface. Which validation will you wire first in your app?

A TransactionFeedback component centralizes how your app displays transaction states and reduces duplicated logic across pages. The component accepts a transactionStatus prop with values such as pending, success, error, and cancelled; a hash prop for the transaction id; and an error prop with a concise message. In practice, you return null when there is no status, and render a styled message area otherwise. Show the hash as plain text for copy or reference, not as an interactive external link, unless you explicitly build a safe link handler. Keep messages short and actionable: for pending, say "Transaction Pending..." and show the hash; for success, say "Transaction Confirmed!" and trigger any necessary UI refresh; for error, summarize the reason and offer retry guidance. In the code example on the screen you will see a clear mapping from status to presentation class names and a helper to truncate the hash for readability. Extract the styling to a small C S S module or Tailwind classes so the component remains framework-agnostic. One common mistake is exposing raw error stacks—avoid that and give users clear next steps instead.

Integrating a TransactionFeedback component into your application involves two practical steps: wiring UI state to the component and disabling inputs while transactions are in-flight. In App. jsx you typically have state such as isSendingTransaction, transactionStatus, and transactionHash from a hook or context. When a user submits a form, call the function that sends the transaction and immediately set the pending state. Disable the form and submit button by binding their disabled attributes to isSendingTransaction. Pass transactionStatus, transactionHash, and any short error to TransactionFeedback so the same component presents the state to the user. The example from the chapter shows a simple flow: connect wallet, show account and balance, render a form that sets new data, and then render TransactionFeedback below the form. A useful pattern is to clear form inputs only after the transaction is sent, not before, to avoid losing the user's input if the send fails. Finally, treat a wallet rejection as a cancelled state and display a short message. This approach keeps users informed, reduces duplicate submissions, and creates a single place to update feedback styling or behavior.

Using small, focused React components keeps your dApp maintainable and consistent. The chapter recommends a set of common components: WalletConnectButton encapsulates detection and connection logic; AccountInfo displays the connected address, balance, and network; TransactionFeedback presents status messages; ContractInteractionForm handles inputs and submission for a specific contract function. Each component has a single responsibility: WalletConnectButton should not render transaction state, and TransactionFeedback should not manage wallet connection. This separation of concerns makes testing and reuse straightforward. For example, reuse TransactionFeedback across pages that submit different transactions; it simply accepts status props. Another useful pattern is placing web3 hooks and context providers near the app root; components then consume the current account and network without duplicating logic. A common mistake is embedding web3 calls inside deeply nested UI components; keep business logic in hooks or the context so components remain declarative. By following these patterns you get code that is easier to audit, extend, and style consistently across the application.
